title: Welcome to the preregistration tutorial!
text:
Tutorial Overview
This self-paced tutorial will introduce you to the key concepts, practices and tools involved in preregistration. Preregistration is an open science practice that is increasingly adopted
intended to take X hours to complete.
The tutorial is split into the following five sections:

Introduction to preregistration provides an introduction to the context of why preregistration exists as an open science practice. This section discusses key concepts and topics such as different research methodologies (e.g. qualitative, experimental, observational), confirmatory vs exploratory analysis, questionable research practices.
How to do a preregistration briefly outlines the essential and recommended elements to include in a study preregistration, with resources to find templates by research method.
Challenges and opportunites of preregistration explores the challenges and opportunities of doing a preregistration from an individual researcher perspective to the wider research ecosystem.

Building a preregistration toolkit provides opportunities to practice improving parts of a study preregistration from research questions to analysis plans.
Evaluating preregistration quality provides guidance and resources to critically evaluate existing preregistration, to equip learners with the tools to complete their own study preregistration.

This tutorial will take you on a journey from:
“I am not sure what preregistration is or why it is important”
to: “I feel empowered to adopt the principles of preregistration”
By the end of this tutorial, you should be able to identify the components of a preregistration, recognize challenges and opportunities of preregistration, propose solutions to navigating barriers to implementing a preregistration and evaluate the quality of a preregistration






TipPrerequisites



This tutorial assumes you have the following:
Familiarity with the steps in the research life cycle, the different types of variables (independent, dependent and covariates)

title: Build up your preregistration toolkit
text:
Research questions and hypotheses

Snippet 1
“How do indoor plants benefit people?”






TipGuiding questions




How would you measure “benefit”?
How would you study the interaction between plants and people?









NoteShow improved answer





How does having physical contact with indoor plants reduce psychological and physiological stress in young-adult office workers?
Notice how the improved answer states the type of interaction between plants and people, more specific details about types of benefits of interest and the target demographic (e.g. young-adult office workers).
Note: This research question is based on a study by Lee et al. 2015





Snippet 2
“We expect that drinking beer will increase reaction time.”






TipGuiding questions




How can information about beer be made more specific?
What is the reaction time measured in relation to?









NoteShow improved answer





For male psychology students, drinking 5 Magic Hat IPAs will increase their reaction time as measured by machine X. We expect that the group that drinks 5 IPAs will respond at least 1 second slower, on average, than the group that did not drink alcohol.
Notice how the improved answer states quantity and type of beer and participants involved in the study. There is also a description about the expected direction of response.

title: Build up your preregistration toolkit
text:
Sampling plan

Snippet 3
“We expect to collect data from 100 subjects.”






TipGuiding questions




Are there any pre-selection rules?
How would you deal with possible exclusions?









NoteShow improved answers





Improved answer 1: We will over sample by 15% in order to account for possible exclusions after we apply exclusion criteria 1 and 2 (see xxx), after 115 participants have started with the study, the computer will redirect the next participants to another task.
Notice how the improved answer states how the researchers apply pre-specified exclusion criteria to reach the expected sample size of 100 subjects.
Alternative improved answer 2: Since data is collected via online survey the final N could result a little higher if further participants answer the questionnaire in the time between reaching N=100 and putting the survey offline, and we will include these extra participants in the final sample.
Notice how the alternative improved answer 2 provides an alternative description of the data collection stopping rule embedding flexibility in the sample size (e.g. including extra participants who answer survey before going offline).
Alternative improved answer 3: We plan to collect usable data from 100 participants. We will schedule slots of up to 10 participants at a time. We anticipate that not all scheduled slots will fill, so we initially will post 150 open slots. If more than 100 participants sign up for the available slots, we will test all of them. Consequently our initial tested sample could include as many as 150 participants. If this initial set of open slots results in testing fewer than 100 participants,we will open additional slots in blocks of 10 until we have tested 100 or more participants in total. We then will evaluate exclusions according to our preregistered rules. If, after exclusion, we have usable data from fewer than 100 participants, we will add enough additional open slots in blocks of 10 to potentially achieve a sample of 100 or more. After completing that testing, we will again evaluate exclusions and will repeat this step as needed until we have usable data from 100 or more participants. Thus, our final sample will include at least 100 participants and up to 150 participants, with the most likely final sample size (given typical signup rates and exclusion rates) between 100 and 109 participants.
Notice how the alternative improved answer 3 provides detailed description of the data collection method (e.g. batching survey slots of 10 participants) and fail-safe procedures for participant exclusions and restarting (e.g. if data on < 100 participants is usable).

title: Build up your preregistration toolkit
text:
Variable description

Snippet 4
“Exam scores for all subjects for final-year bachelor students.”






TipGuiding questions




How can information about the exam scores be more specific?
Is it clear which point in the school year exam scores are measured?









NoteShow improved answer





Average exam scores for all subjects for final-year bachelor students at the end of the first term after the intervention.
Notice how the improved answer states how and when the variable is measured.

title: Build up your preregistration toolkit
text:
Design plan

Snippet 5
“Light levels will be manipulated four different ways over the 20 seedling growing trays.”






TipGuiding questions




Is there enough information to understand how the light levels are manipulated?









NoteShow improved answer





Light manipulation will be initiated at seed planting stage (day 0) and run continuously until the end of experiment (day 90). The light manipulation is implemented as a randomized, replicated block design in which four light treatments are repeated across five blocks (n = 20 seedling trays). One of the four light treatments (ambient control, procedural control, -25% light, and +25% light, with respect to ambient light levels) will be applied at the seedling tray level which is nested into the blocks. Adding a procedural control tests the effect of the light manipulation equipment (e.g. potential confounding effect of light treatment).
Notice how the improved answer states the experimental procedures and structure (e.g. randomized replicated block design) and levels of the variables.

title: Build up your preregistration toolkit
text:
Exclusions and exceptions

Snippet 6
“We will exclude participants who take too long to answer survey and score low on x.”






TipGuiding questions




How long is too long to answer survey defined?
What counts as a low score?









NoteShow improved answer





We will exclude participants who do not pass two thirds of the attention checks and if time taken to complete the survey is outside the range of 10-20 minutes. Participants will also be excluded if they score below 12 on x.
Notice how the improved answer specifies how long is too long to answer survey (i.e. data-based outlier criteria) and defined score level for x (i.e. method-based outlier criteria).

title: Build up your preregistration toolkit
text:
Analysis plan

Snippet 7
“A two (Design: simple, complex) by two (group: manipulated, control) mixed ANOVA will be the designated statistical analysis. This statistical analysis will provide insight into the 2-way interaction between the Design (simple vs complex) and group (manipulated or control).”






TipGuiding questions




Would a reader be able to carry out this ANOVA as described?









NoteShow ways to improve answer





Provide statistical model expression/code, which makes it explicit to the readers the model structure and syntax used to run your analysis. Provide analysis of simulated data and plot/interpret the results (this allows you to think whether design is strong enough to conclude something meaningful whatever the results are).

title: Build up your preregistration toolkit
text:
Reporting study preregistration

Snippet 8
“Hypothesis:… We aimed to test (1) whether abstract thinking is positively correlated with autonomous motivation … Conclusion:… BIF scores (abstract thinking) were positively associated with trait self-control, autonomous motivation for exercise, and autonomous motivation for diet, but not with sugar or fried food consumption…”






TipGuiding questions




Do the results reported in the study match to the hypothesis stated?









NoteShow ways to improve answer





Link study outcomes explicitly to numbered hypotheses and contextualize them to the variables, to allow readers to more easily follow. State clearly any unplanned analyses or deviations from what was preregistered.

title: Build up your preregistration toolkit
text:
Extension excercise
If you want more practice at doing a preregistration, have a go at filling out a preregistration template using the platform AsPredicted. A version of this extension exercise is available as a worksheet here (LINK).
The aim is to increase your familiarity with the process of filling out a study preregistration and noting down any challenges while you practice. For this exercise you can draw from your own research project and have a go at filling the 11 questions in 20 minutes. 20 minutes should be sufficient time to get a taster for the process. Use the reflection questions below to help you think about your experience of completing this exercise.
As your confidence and learning progresses you can have a go at a more comprehensive study preregistration template like the Open Science Framework (OSF).






TipReflection questions




Did you go through the questions in order?
Were there any questions you were not expecting?
What was the most challenging part of the preregistration process?

title: Challenges and opportunities of preregistration
section: Time: “I haven’t got time to do a study registration”
text:
Time: “I haven’t got time to do a study registration”
The time and effort needed to do a preregistration is a frequently cited challenge, especially in a ‘publish or perish’ research culture. There is a some truth to this statement, as study planning should take time. Reframing the upfront time investment as a
Counterargument: front-loaded effort during the planning stage can help later on during write up and during peer review.

objectID: Challenges and opportunities of preregistration/Challenges and opportunities.html#lack-of-incentives-i-dont-see-the-point
href: Challenges and opportunities of preregistration/Challenges and opportunities.html#lack-of-incentives-i-dont-see-the-point
title: Challenges and opportunities of preregistration
section: Lack of incentives: “I don’t see the point”
text:
Lack of incentives: “I don’t see the point”
Counterargument: aside from individual researcher benefits (increased reflection, reduced likelihood of systematic errors), journals are increasingly prioritizing study registrations.

objectID: Challenges and opportunities of preregistration/Challenges and opportunities.html#overwhelm-there-is-so-much-that-goes-into-a-study-registration
href: Challenges and opportunities of preregistration/Challenges and opportunities.html#overwhelm-there-is-so-much-that-goes-into-a-study-registration
title: Challenges and opportunities of preregistration
section: Overwhelm: “There is so much that goes into a study registration”
text:
Overwhelm: “There is so much that goes into a study registration”
Counterargument: templates and FAQ pages can guide you and if you are unable to officially register a study, adopting principles of study registration is a good step (e.g. Open Science Buffet approach, @bergma2023)

Lack of support: “No one in my team knows or cares about study
registration”
Counterargument: share resources, and suggest a group meeting to discuss and learn more about study registration to increase familiarity.

objectID: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html
href: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html
title: Components of a preregistration
text: Recap: In the introduction we covered the context and rationale of preregistration. Here we will learn what the practical steps involved are and what information is required to complete a study preregistration.

objectID: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#part-1-hypotheses
href: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#part-1-hypotheses
title: Components of a preregistration
text:
Part 1: Hypotheses
Essential:

State your research questions clearly
Describe the (numbered) hypotheses in the context of your variables
For interaction effects, describe the expected shape of the interactions.
If you are manipulating a variable, make predictions for successful check variables or explain why no manipulation check is included.

Recommendations:

Adding a table/figure to describe complex interaction
For studies testing hypotheses, link stated hypotheses to theoretical frameworks

objectID: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#part-2-design
href: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#part-2-design
title: Components of a preregistration
text:
Part 2: Design
Essential:
List of variables based on your hypotheses:

Independent variables (including levels, within or between participants, relationship between them (e.g. nested))
dependent variables or variables in a correlational design
third variables (e.g. covariates, moderators, control variables)

objectID: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#part-3-planned-sample
href: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#part-3-planned-sample
title: Components of a preregistration
text:
Part 3: Planned sample
Essential:

If applicable, state any pre-selection rules (e.g. age limits)
Indicate where, from whom and how the data will be collected
Justify planned sample size (e.g. power analysis)
Describe data collection termination rule

objectID: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#part-4-exclusion-criteria
href: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#part-4-exclusion-criteria
title: Components of a preregistration
text:
Part 4: Exclusion criteria
Essential:
Describe anticipated specific data exclusion criteria such as:

missing, erroneous, or overly consistent responses
failing check-tests or suspicion probes
demographic exclusions
data-based outlier criteria (e.g expected variable ranges)
method-based outlier criteria (e.g. too short or long response times)

Recommendations:

Set fail-safe levels of exclusion at which the whole study needs to be stopped, altered, and restarted.

objectID: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#part-5-analysis-plan
href: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#part-5-analysis-plan
title: Components of a preregistration
text:
Part 5: Analysis plan
Essential:
Describe the analyses that will test each main prediction from the hypotheses section. For each one, include:

relevant variables and how they are calculated
statistical technique
each variable’s role in the technique (e.g., independent variable, dependent variable and covariates)
rationale for each covariate used, if any
if using techniques other than null hypothesis testing (e.g. Bayesian statistics), describe your criteria calculation of prior values or distributions

Recommendations:

Specify contingencies and assumptions (e.g. method of correcting for multiple testing, missing data handling, data transformations (e.g. Shapiro-Wilk’s test for normal/Gaussian distribution), assumptions and assumption checks for analyses and alternative plans for data analysis if assumptions are not met).

objectID: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#additional-considerations
href: How to do a preregistration/Preregistration components.html#additional-considerations
title: Components of a preregistration
text:
Additional considerations
Depending on your study type, there may be additional things to keep in mind as you plan your study. You’ll need to determine if you need to: plan for multi-stage contingent experiments, anonymize your registration (e.g. place under embargo) or apply for ethical approval.

title: Components of a preregistration
text:
Preregistration vs registered reports
So far content has focused on preregistration, but there is another related Open Science practice known as a registered report. Registered reports are a publishing format where a study undergoes two stages of peer review: stage 1: introduction and methods in advance of data collection/analysis and stage 2: which includes the full study findings including results/discussion (Parsons et al. 2022). Registered reports can help safeguard against finding potential study design issues after data collection.






Warning



You may come across registered reports being described in the literature as “two-stage review with in-principle acceptance” [@mayo-wilson2025]. Some meta-science researchers are working calling for the Open Science community to harmonize terms to reduce ambiguity.

title: Introduction to preregistration
text:
When reading a typical journal article, can you tell if the research questions or hypotheses were formulated before or after the study findings were known, and does this matter? Short answer is: no you can’t really tell and yes it does matter! Recognizing the difference between predictions and postdictions both as a contributor to and consumer of research is critical for transparent and credible science (Nosek et al 2018). Conflating predictions and postdictions can lead to… Presenting postdictions as predictions can increase publishability of findings (e.g. positive and novel results) by falsely reducing uncertainty….
Preregistration is a practice which aims to clarify prediction vs postdiction in a research study. This is works by producing an uneditable time-stamped document that outlines a study plan including research questions/hypotheses, research design, data analysis before data collection and analysis. A study preregistration is then uploaded onto a verified repository so that it can be publicly shared with others (possibly after an embargo period) (Nosek, 2018; Parsons et al. 2022). Importantly, preregistration remains agnostic when it comes to prediction vs postdiction approach to research, it aims to clearly differentiate between the two.






WarningTerminology



You may notice in the literature different terms relating to preregistration like study registration. Some researchers are advocating for a reform of terms to avoid ambiguity, as some terms can refer to different practices occurring at various stages of the research life cycle [@mayo-wilson2025]. In this tutorial, we will use the term preregistration.

title: Introduction to preregistration
text:
Approaches to research
There is no single one way to do research! It all depends on what information you are trying to gather. Research can be:

Qualitative (interview study, focus groups, ethnographic)
Review-based (systematic, narrative)
Intervention/experimental (randomized control trials, factorial design)
Observational (case study, natural experiment, longitudinal)







NoteWhat is your research approach?



Being able to understand the different research approaches, study designs and key concepts will help provide context for the steps required to do a study registration.

title: Introduction to preregistration
text:
What would you do?
Imagine if your PhD lab mate Max came to you with this dilemma: “I’ve been analyzing the data from my first thesis chapter (which I really want to publish, as it will help with my chances of getting a post doc). One of my hypotheses is that X influences Y. I’ve measured many variables to test this hypothesis. However during the data analysis, results seem to show X has no effect on Y, unless I remove a variable. Do you have any suggestions of what I should do?”
What would you recommend Max does from the options listed below? A) Remove that variable from the analysis B) Tweak the hypothesis to match the results C) Collect more data in the hope, a larger sample size will show an effect D) Try out a new statistical test to see if there is a significant effect E) Leave that variable in and write up the results as they are
We will revisit Max’s dilemma throughout this tutorial and hopefully by the end you will be more confident at identifying potential issues and recognize how preregistration can help safeguard against questionable research practice and promote more credible research.






TipSummary

title: Research cycle
text:
Qualitative research approaches focus on examining the meanings, experiences, and perspectives of individuals or groups. Data collection involves primary, first-hand, text-based data that is analyzed using specific interpretive methods. Sometimes text-based data is ‘coded’ to identify key themes and patterns (Braun and Clarke 2008).



Review-based research involves collating and synthesizing previously published work on a topic. These approaches can be used to generate new insights and identify knowledge gaps. Reviews can be more or less done systematically, with systematic review and meta-analyses having well-established protocols (e.g. PRISMA guidelines).



Intervention and experimental research approaches are closely related. They involve deliberate manipulations to a physical entity (e.g. individuals, groups, organisms) intended to measure changes to that entity. Intervention studies typically focuses on the application of a treatment or action to observe its effect. In experimental studies, a researcher typically observes a problem or situation, then develops a testable hypothesis from which experiments under controlled conditions are used to test specific hypotheses. Based on the outcomes, the hypothesis is adapted. A hypothesis is an unproven statement relating the connection between variables.






NoteHypothesis generating vs testing



Hypothesis generating vs testing are two modes of research inquiry that influence study designs and underpin the practice of study registrations. Hypothesis generating: - exploratory, discovery-focused research (asks questions like: what is happening? Why is it happening, How is it happening?)
Hypothesis testing: - confirmatory, justification-focused research (asks questions like: what does X do to Y?)
The distinctions between hypothesis generating vs testing research are often not clearly differentiated in practice, which leads to questionable research practices and reduced credibility of research.





Observational research gathers information about individuals or populations without manipulating the environment or variables. Researchers observe and collect data on subjects as they naturally occur in their usual settings. An example of observational research:



For research that adopts one or more theoretical frameworks (social and biological sciences) or data types (e.g. participant surveys, visual data, geospatial), would be described as a mixed-method approach.

title: Questionable research practices and biases
text:
From one end of the research integrity spectrum of clear misconduct (e.g. falsifying results or plagiarizing someones work) to acceptable and responsible research practices (i.e. what Open Science movement strives to create), where do the selective reporting or misrepresentations of data fit in? This grey zone of Questionable Research Practices (QRPs) of less overt and subtle behaviors (compared to misconduct) nonetheless damages the credibility of science (). The prevalence and impact of QRPs has received less attention than the clear cut examples of serious research misconduct (although see case study below)


Hypothesizing after the results are known (HARKing) is a QRP where a researcher changes their hypothesis based on or informed by the results, but present their hypothesis as if it were a priori [@kerr1998].



p-Hacking is a QRP which describes the many ways researchers can artificially increase the likelihood of obtaining a statistically significant result [@pennington2023].






NoteCase study



https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0339056

title: Questionable research practices and biases
text:
Hindsight bias
The “I knew it all along” is the phrase associated with hindsight bias, which is the tendency to frame previous decisions or events as more predictable after the outcome is known [@hardwicke2023].

title: Questionable research practices and biases
text:
Confirmatory bias
The tendency to seek out, interpret, favor and recall information in a way that supports one’s prior values, beliefs, expectations, or hypothesis [@parsons2022].

title: Questionable research practices and biases
text:
Bias blind spot
The lack of awareness of how one’s decisions are shaped by bias [@hardwicke2023].
The range of biases highlights that we are all human and it is important to be aware of how cognitive biases influence how we do our research!

title: Frequently asked questions
text: This section contains a collection of common misconceptions, frequently asked questions and concerns around preregistration. This collection is organized according to the stages of doing a preregistration. It is designed to be used as a reference guide which you can revisit.

title: Frequently asked questions
text:
Thinking about doing a preregistration
I’m a student starting a new project and I feel I don’t know enough to do a good preregistration, is it worth doing one?






TipAnswer





Answer



The data I am working with is descriptive, is a study preregistration still useful?






TipAnswer





Answer



I work with secondary data and I know what my data look like, what is the point of doing a preregistration?






TipAnswer





It is possible to preregister an analysis plan for studies that use secondary data! There are many benefits to preregistration of secondary data that overlap with general benefits of preregistration (e.g. distinguishing between confirmatory and exploratory analysis, mitigating researcher degrees of freedom). See a template for preregistration of secondary data by Mertens and Krypotos (2019).



Is it true that doing a preregistration increases the risk of being scooped?






TipAnswer





Concerns around being scooped can be mitigated by putting an embargo on your preregistration which will make it private until you are ready to share it. Depending on the platform used to upload your preregistration, it can be private indefinitely (e.g. AsPredicted) or a maximum or 4 years from creation date for Open Science Foundation. In addition, by preregistering you are informing others your research plans and they are unlikely to put time, effort and resources to do the same study as you.
